preamble: In French, the Old French diphthong ie produced by Bartsch's law (Latin stressed a after a palatal: cārum > chier) and by diphthongization of ĕ became [je]. The glide was then lost in most words: it was absorbed by a preceding palatal consonant or removed by analogy in -er verbs. The glide survived only where nasalization followed (chien [ʃjɛ̃]). The result merged with the e from the general fronting of a (mer, porter). In closed syllables the outcome is open [ɛ] (cher [ʃɛʁ], chef [ʃɛf]); word-finally it is close [e].

examples.note: [ie] > [je] > [e] in the infinitive ending -ier after a palatal.
The glide was absorbed by the preceding palatal; -ier > -er spread analogically to other first-conjugation verbs.
Same reduction; in a closed syllable the vowel is open [ɛ].

sources: Bourciez, É., & Bourciez, J. (1967). Phonétique française: étude historique. Paris: Klincksieck.
